title: Classification of Elements and Periodicity

toc.title: 3.1 Modern periodic law and table; s, p, d and f blocks; isoelectronic species
3.2 Periodic trends: size, ionisation energy, electronegativity, electron affinity and metallic character

html:
Periodicity carries about one question in the paper (our estimate from the MEC topic list), but its trends are used again in bonding, s-block, non-metal and transition-metal questions. The question is almost always one of four kinds: locate an element (period, group, block) from its atomic number, put a set of atoms or ions in order of a property, explain an exception (Be > B, N > O, Cl > F), or read successive ionisation energies. Everything follows from two ideas — effective nuclear charge and the number of shells.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • Modern periodic law (Moseley): properties are periodic functions of atomic number.
  • Period = highest shell number; block = subshell receiving the last electron; group from the valence electrons (s: ns; p: 10 + ns + np; d: ns + (n − 1)d).
  • Isoelectronic species: same electrons, so the radius falls as the nuclear charge rises (N³⁻ > O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺ > Al³⁺).
  • Across a period: size ↓, ionisation energy ↑, electronegativity ↑, electron affinity ↑, metallic character ↓; down a group the reverse.
  • Exceptions: IE Be > B and N > O (also Mg > Al, P > S); EA Cl > F and S > O; Ga is smaller than Al; Zr ≈ Hf (lanthanoid contraction).
  • Superlatives: He highest IE, Cs lowest (stable elements); F most electronegative (4.0); Cl highest electron affinity.

3.1 Modern periodic law and table; s, p, d and f blocks; isoelectronic species

From Mendeleev to Moseley

Mendeleev (1869) arranged the elements by increasing atomic mass and grouped elements with similar properties. He left gaps and predicted the properties of undiscovered elements — eka-boron (Sc), eka-aluminium (Ga) and eka-silicon (Ge). But he had to reverse some pairs to keep the chemistry right (Ar 39.9 before K 39.1; Co before Ni; Te before I), and isotopes had no place. Moseley (1913) found that the square root of the frequency of an element's characteristic X-rays is proportional to its atomic number, \sqrt{\nu} = a(Z - b). Ordered by Z, every reversal disappears.

Modern periodic law

The physical and chemical properties of the elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.

The cause of periodicity is the repetition of similar outer electronic configurations after intervals of 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32 and 32 elements.

The long form of the table

The modern table has 7 periods and 18 groups (IUPAC numbering 1–18) and holds 118 elements. The period number is the principal quantum number of the outermost shell.

Period Subshells filled Elements Description
1 1s 2 very short
2, 3 ns np 8 each short
4, 5 ns (n − 1)d np 18 each long
6, 7 ns (n − 2)f (n − 1)d np 32 each very long
Group Family Valence configuration
1 alkali metals (H is placed here but is not one) ns¹
2 alkaline earth metals ns²
3–12 transition metals (n − 1)d¹⁻¹⁰ ns⁰⁻²
13 boron family ns² np¹
14 carbon family ns² np²
15 nitrogen family (pnictogens) ns² np³
16 oxygen family (chalcogens) ns² np⁴
17 halogens ns² np⁵
18 noble gases ns² np⁶ (He 1s²)

The four blocks

Block Last (differentiating) electron enters General configuration Position Character
s ns ns¹⁻² groups 1, 2 (and He) reactive metals, low IE, fixed valency, ionic compounds, basic oxides
p np ns² np¹⁻⁶ groups 13–18 metals, metalloids and non-metals; most variable oxidation states
d (n − 1)d (n − 1)d¹⁻¹⁰ ns⁰⁻² groups 3–12, periods 4–7 transition metals: variable oxidation states, coloured ions, complexes, catalysts
f (n − 2)f (n − 2)f¹⁻¹⁴ (n − 1)d⁰⁻¹ ns² two rows below the table inner transition: lanthanoids (4f, Z = 58–71) and actinoids (5f, Z = 90–103, all radioactive)

The representative (main-group) elements are the s- and p-block elements other than the noble gases. Metalloids (B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te) lie on the diagonal staircase between metals and non-metals. Helium is 1s² — an s-block configuration — but sits in group 18 because its shell is complete and it is inert like the other noble gases.

Locating an element from its atomic number

Write the configuration; the period is the highest n; the block is the subshell that received the last electron; the group is the number of ns electrons (s-block), 10 + the ns and np electrons (p-block), or the ns + (n − 1)d electrons (d-block). All f-block elements belong to group 3.

Noble-gas shortcut. Subtract the atomic number of the previous noble gas (2, 10, 18, 36, 54, 86). The remainder is the element's place in the next period. In periods 4 and 5 that place is the group number. In periods 6 and 7 places 4–17 are the f-block, and from place 18 onwards subtract 14 to get the group.

Period, group and block in ten seconds

Problem. Locate the elements with Z = 33, 26 and 82.

Solution. Z = 33: 33 − 18 = 15th place in period 4 → period 4, group 15, p-block (arsenic, [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p³). Z = 26: [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s², 6 + 2 = 8 → period 4, group 8, d-block (iron). Z = 82: 82 − 54 = 28th place in period 6; 28 − 14 = 14 → period 6, group 14, p-block (lead).

IUPAC names for Z > 100. Read the digits with the roots 0 nil, 1 un, 2 bi, 3 tri, 4 quad, 5 pent, 6 hex, 7 sept, 8 oct, 9 enn, and add -ium; the symbol is the first letters of the three roots. Z = 104 → un-nil-quad-ium, unnilquadium (Unq) (now rutherfordium); Z = 114 → ununquadium (Uuq) (now flerovium); Z = 120 → unbinilium (Ubn). (The final "i" of bi and tri is dropped before -ium.)

Isoelectronic species

Isoelectronic species

Atoms, ions or molecules that contain the same number of electrons (usually with the same configuration) are isoelectronic.

Electrons Isoelectronic set
2 H⁻, He, Li⁺, Be²⁺
10 N³⁻, O²⁻, F⁻, Ne, Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺; CH₄, NH₃, H₂O, HF, NH₄⁺, H₃O⁺, OH⁻
14 N₂, CO, CN⁻, NO⁺, C₂²⁻
18 P³⁻, S²⁻, Cl⁻, Ar, K⁺, Ca²⁺; HCl, H₂S, PH₃, SiH₄
22 CO₂, N₂O, N₃⁻, NO₂⁺

In an isoelectronic series the same number of electrons is held by an increasing number of protons, so the radius decreases as Z increases: N³⁻ > O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺ > Al³⁺ and S²⁻ > Cl⁻ > K⁺ > Ca²⁺. Quick rule: the more negative the charge, the larger the species.

3.2 Periodic trends: size, ionisation energy, electronegativity, electron affinity and metallic character

The two causes behind every trend

Effective nuclear charge, Z_{eff} = Z - \sigma, is the nuclear charge actually felt by an outer electron after the inner electrons have screened (shielded) part of it (σ is the screening constant). Screening power falls in the order s > p > d > f.

  • Across a period Z rises by one at each step, but the new electron goes into the same shell and screens poorly, so Z_eff rises and the outer electrons are pulled closer.
  • Down a group a new shell is added each period; the larger distance and extra screening outweigh the larger nuclear charge.

Atomic radius

Atomic radius is measured as the covalent radius (half the distance between two identical atoms joined by a single bond), the metallic radius (half the distance between neighbouring atoms in a metal) or the van der Waals radius (half the distance of closest approach of non-bonded atoms). For one element, van der Waals radius > covalent radius (Cl: 180 pm against 99 pm). Noble gases have only van der Waals radii, so they cannot be compared fairly with the rest of their period.

Period 3 Na Mg Al Si P S Cl
Atomic radius (pm) 186 160 143 117 110 104 99
IE₁ (kJ mol⁻¹) 496 738 578 787 1012 1000 1251
Electronegativity 0.9 1.2 1.5 1.8 2.1 2.5 3.0

Down group 1 the radius grows: Li 152, Na 186, K 227, Rb 248, Cs 265 pm. Two exceptions are popular:

  • Ga (135 pm) is smaller than Al (143 pm): the ten 3d electrons added before gallium shield the nucleus poorly, so Z_eff is higher than expected.
  • Lanthanoid contraction: across the fourteen 4f elements the radius falls steadily, because 4f electrons shield very poorly. The 5d metals after them are therefore almost the same size as the 4d metals above them — Zr (160 pm) ≈ Hf (159 pm) — and so are chemically very similar.

Ionic radius

Rule Example
A cation is smaller than its atom (fewer electrons, often one shell fewer, same nuclear charge) Na⁺ is about half the size of Na
An anion is larger than its atom (more electron repulsion, same nuclear charge) Cl 99 pm, Cl⁻ 181 pm
The higher the positive charge, the smaller the ion Fe > Fe²⁺ > Fe³⁺; Pb²⁺ > Pb⁴⁺
Isoelectronic ions: higher Z, smaller ion O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺
Down a group ions grow Li⁺ < Na⁺ < K⁺ < Rb⁺ < Cs⁺; F⁻ < Cl⁻ < Br⁻ < I⁻

Ionisation energy

Ionisation energy (ionisation enthalpy)

The first ionisation energy is the minimum energy needed to remove the most loosely held electron from an isolated gaseous atom in its ground state: M(g) → M⁺(g) + e⁻. It is quoted in kJ mol⁻¹ or in eV per atom (1 eV per atom = 96.5 kJ mol⁻¹).

It rises with nuclear charge and with a stable (half-filled or filled) configuration; it falls with atomic size and with screening; and an s electron (more penetrating) is harder to remove than a p electron of the same shell. Hence IE increases across a period and decreases down a group: He (2372 kJ mol⁻¹) is the highest of all; Cs (376) is the lowest among the stable elements.

The two dips everyone is asked about
  • Be (899) > B (801) and Mg > Al: boron's electron is a 2p electron, higher in energy and shielded by the filled 2s² pair, so it is easier to remove.
  • N (1402) > O (1314) and P > S: nitrogen's 2p³ is half-filled and extra stable; in oxygen the fourth 2p electron is paired, and repulsion between the paired electrons makes it easier to remove. So across period 2 the order is Li < B < Be < C < O < N < F < Ne — not a smooth rise.

Successive ionisation energies always increase (IE₁ < IE₂ < IE₃ …), because each electron is removed from an ion that is more positive. A very large jump means the next electron has to come from a complete inner shell — so the number of electrons removed before the jump is the number of valence electrons.

Reading successive ionisation energies

Problem. An element has IE₁ to IE₄ = 578, 1817, 2745 and 11 577 kJ mol⁻¹. To which group does it belong?

Solution. The ratios IE₂/IE₁ ≈ 3.1 and IE₃/IE₂ ≈ 1.5 are modest, but IE₄/IE₃ ≈ 4.2 is the big jump: three electrons come off easily, the fourth comes from a noble-gas core. Three valence electrons → group 13 (it is aluminium).

Electron affinity (electron gain enthalpy)

Electron affinity

Electron affinity is the energy released when an electron is added to an isolated gaseous atom in its ground state: X(g) + e⁻ → X⁻(g). The electron gain enthalpy ΔegH is the same quantity with the opposite sign: a large electron affinity means a large negative ΔegH.

Electron affinity generally increases across a period (higher Z_eff, smaller atom) and decreases down a group. The exceptions are examined more often than the rule:

Fact Reason
Cl (349) > F (328) > Br (325) > I (295) kJ mol⁻¹ F is so small that its compact 2p shell repels the incoming electron strongly
S (200) > O (141) the same small-size effect in oxygen
Noble gases: ΔegH positive (energy absorbed) the electron would have to enter a new shell
Be, Mg and N: almost zero or slightly negative EA filled ns² or half-filled np³ subshells are stable
Every second EA is negative (O⁻ + e⁻ → O²⁻ absorbs energy) the electron is added to an ion that is already negative

Halogens have the highest electron affinities of all, because one electron completes their octet; chlorine has the highest of all elements.

Electronegativity

Electronegativity

Electronegativity is the tendency of an atom in a molecule to attract the shared pair of electrons towards itself. It is a relative number with no unit. On Pauling's scale fluorine = 4.0. Mulliken defined it as the average of the ionisation energy and the electron affinity.

It increases across a period and decreases down a group: **F 4.0 > O 3.5 > N 3.0 ≈ Cl 3.0

Br 2.8 > C 2.5 ≈ S 2.5 ≈ I 2.5 > H 2.1**; the least electronegative are Cs and Fr (0.7). An atom's electronegativity rises with its oxidation state and with the s character of its hybrid orbital (sp > sp² > sp³).

Electronegativity Electron affinity
Refers to an atom bonded in a molecule an isolated gaseous atom
Nature a relative tendency an energy change
Unit none (Pauling scale) kJ mol⁻¹ or eV
Highest F Cl

Metallic character, oxides and the diagonal relationship

Metallic character (electropositivity) is the tendency of an atom to lose electrons. It falls across a period and rises down a group, the opposite of ionisation energy. The oxides follow it: across period 3, Na₂O and MgO are basic, Al₂O₃ is amphoteric (it reacts with both acids and alkalis), and SiO₂ (weakly), P₄O₁₀, SO₃ and Cl₂O₇ (strongly) are acidic. Down a group the oxides and hydroxides become more basic (Be(OH)₂ is amphoteric, Ba(OH)₂ a strong alkali). The diagonal relationship — Li with Mg, Be with Al, B with Si — arises because the diagonal pairs have similar size-to-charge ratios (polarising power).

Property Across a period → Down a group ↓
Atomic and ionic radius decreases increases
Ionisation energy increases (dips at groups 13 and 16) decreases
Electron affinity increases (Cl > F) decreases
Electronegativity increases decreases
Metallic character, reducing power decreases increases
Non-metallic character, oxidising power increases decreases
Basic character of oxides decreases increases
Ordering questions in one pass

Put the species on the periodic table in your head. For size, ionisation energy and electronegativity, decide position first (period beats group: going down one shell changes size more than moving one place across), then check the exceptions list — Be/B, N/O, Mg/Al, P/S, Cl/F, Ga/Al. If two options differ only in one adjacent pair, that pair is the exception the setter is testing.

Formula and fact sheet

Moseley's law \sqrt{\nu} = a(Z - b)

Noble-gas atomic numbers 2, 10, 18, 36, 54, 86, 118

Effective nuclear charge Z_{eff} = Z - \sigma; screening s > p > d > f

Mulliken electronegativity (IE + EA)/2
IUPAC roots 0 nil, 1 un, 2 bi, 3 tri, 4 quad, 5 pent, 6 hex, 7 sept, 8 oct, 9 enn + ium
Numbers worth knowing
IE₁, period 2 (kJ mol⁻¹) Li 520, Be 899, B 801, C 1086, N 1402, O 1314, F 1681, Ne 2081
IE₁ extremes He 2372 (highest), H 1312, Cs 376 (lowest stable)
Electron affinity (kJ mol⁻¹) Cl 349 > F 328 > Br 325 > I 295; S 200 > O 141

Chapter summary

  • Modern periodic law: properties are periodic functions of atomic number; periodicity comes from the recurrence of similar outer configurations.
  • 7 periods (2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32 elements) and 18 groups; s, p, d and f blocks by the subshell that takes the last electron; He is s-block but sits in group 18.
  • Group from configuration: s-block ns electrons, p-block 10 + ns + np, d-block ns + (n − 1)d.
  • Isoelectronic species share an electron count; their radius falls as Z rises.
  • Across a period Z_eff rises: size falls; IE, EA and electronegativity rise; metallic character and basic character of oxides fall. Down a group the reverse.
  • IE exceptions Be > B, N > O (Mg > Al, P > S); EA exceptions Cl > F, S > O; noble gases, Be, Mg and N have near-zero or negative EA.
  • Highest IE He, lowest Cs; most electronegative F (4.0); highest EA Cl. A big jump in successive IEs counts the valence electrons.
  • Ga < Al in size (poor 3d shielding); Zr ≈ Hf (lanthanoid contraction).

Practice questions

Answers and explanations — Set A

1. (b) — Moseley showed atomic number, not atomic mass, is the fundamental property; ordering by mass forced Mendeleev to reverse pairs such as Ar and K.

2. (d) — Moseley's law, √ν = a(Z − b), linked X-ray frequency to atomic number (1913). Mendeleev's law (1869) was based on atomic mass.

3. (a) — Period 4 fills 4s, 3d and 4p: 2 + 10 + 6 = 18 elements (K to Kr).

4. (c) — The lanthanoids and actinoids fill (n − 2)f orbitals: inner transition elements. "Transition elements" are the d-block.

5. (c) — Fluorine, 4.0 on the Pauling scale. Oxygen (3.5) is second.

6. (a) — Chlorine (349 kJ mol⁻¹) beats fluorine (328), whose tiny 2p shell repels the added electron.

7. (b) — Helium (2372 kJ mol⁻¹): a 1s² pair held by two protons with no screening. Neon is next (2081).

8. (d) — Ionisation energy falls down group 1 as size grows; Cs (376 kJ mol⁻¹) is the lowest of these.

9. (b) — The nuclear charge rises while electrons enter the same shell, so Z_eff rises and pulls the shell in.

10. (a) — Silicon is a metalloid (semiconductor); Na is a metal, S and Cl are non-metals.

11. (d) — Isoelectronic means "equal electrons" (e.g. Na⁺, Ne and F⁻ have 10 each).

12. (c) — 1-0-4 → un-nil-quad-ium: unnilquadium, symbol Unq (now rutherfordium). Ununquadium is element 114.

13. (a) — Zinc ([Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s²) is in group 12 of the d-block. Ga and Ge are p-block, Ca is s-block.

14. (d) — Group 16 (O, S, Se, Te, Po) are the chalcogens ("ore-formers"); pnictogens are group 15, halogens group 17.

15. (b) — Poor screening by the 4f electrons shrinks the elements after the lanthanoids, so Hf (5d) ends up the size of Zr (4d).

16. (c) — Al₂O₃ dissolves in acids and in alkalis. Na₂O and MgO are basic; SO₃ is acidic.

17. (d) — With fewer electrons for the same nuclear charge (and often one shell fewer), a cation is always smaller than its atom.

18. (a) — The second electron is removed from a positive ion, which holds its electrons more tightly.

19. (c) — By configuration helium is s-block, but its complete shell and inertness place it with the noble gases. It has two valence electrons, not eight.

20. (b) — F = 4.0 on Pauling's scale; 3.5 is oxygen, 3.0 nitrogen or chlorine, 2.8 bromine.

Set B — Understanding (13 questions)

  1. The correct order of atomic radius isaSi > Al > Mg > NabMg > Na > Si > AlcNa > Mg > Al > SidAl > Si > Na > Mg
  2. The correct order of first ionisation energy isaB < Be < C < O < NbBe < B < C < N < OcB < Be < C < N < OdBe < B < C < O < N
  3. Nitrogen has a higher first ionisation energy than oxygen becauseanitrogen is the larger atomboxygen has a higher nuclear chargecoxygen is more electronegativednitrogen has a half-filled, extra-stable 2p³ subshell
  4. Chlorine has a higher electron affinity than fluorine becauseachlorine has a higher nuclear chargebfluorine's compact 2p shell repels the added electroncfluorine is less electronegativedchlorine has fewer shells

  9. The correct order of size isaFe³⁺ > Fe²⁺ > FebFe²⁺ > Fe > Fe³⁺cFe > Fe²⁺ > Fe³⁺dFe = Fe²⁺ = Fe³⁺
  10. Gallium has a slightly smaller atomic radius than aluminium becauseaits ten 3d electrons shield the nucleus poorlybit has fewer shells than aluminiumcit is a non-metaldit has a lower nuclear charge
  11. Which statement about electronegativity and electron affinity is correct?aboth are measured in kJ mol⁻¹belectronegativity refers to an isolated gaseous atomcelectron affinity refers to an atom in a bonddelectronegativity refers to a bonded atom and has no unit
  12. Which oxide is the most basic?aAl₂O₃bNa₂OcMgOdSiO₂
  13. The electron gain enthalpy of a noble gas is positive (energy is absorbed) becauseanoble gases have the largest atoms in their periodsbnoble gases have the highest electronegativitiescthe added electron must enter a new, higher shelldnoble gases have low nuclear charges
Answers and explanations — Set B

1. (c) — Across period 3 the radius falls: Na 186, Mg 160, Al 143, Si 117 pm.

2. (a) — B 801 < Be 899 < C 1086 < O 1314 < N 1402 kJ mol⁻¹: boron dips below beryllium and oxygen below nitrogen.

3. (d) — The half-filled 2p³ subshell is extra stable; oxygen's paired 2p electron is repelled by its partner and leaves more easily. Being larger (a) would lower, not raise, the IE.

4. (b) — Fluorine's 2p shell is so small and crowded that the incoming electron is strongly repelled. Cl's higher nuclear charge is largely screened by its extra shell.

5. (a) — All have 10 electrons; O²⁻ has the fewest protons (8) holding them, so it is the largest.

6. (c) — CO (6 + 8) and N₂ (7 + 7) both have 14 electrons. NO has 15; Na⁺ 10 vs K⁺ 18; F⁻ 10 vs Cl⁻ 18.

7. (d) — Z = 35: [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p⁵ — period 4, p-block, group 10 + 7 = 17 (bromine).

8. (b) — d-block group = ns + (n − 1)d electrons = 1 + 5 = 6 (chromium).

9. (c) — Removing electrons lets the same nucleus pull the rest closer; the more electrons removed, the smaller the species.

10. (a) — The filled 3d¹⁰ shells poorly, so gallium's outer electrons feel a higher effective nuclear charge. Ga has more shells than Al, and a higher Z.

11. (d) — Electronegativity is a relative tendency of a bonded atom (no unit); electron affinity is an energy of an isolated gaseous atom.

12. (b) — Metallic character, and so basic character of the oxide, is greatest at the left of a period: Na₂O > MgO > Al₂O₃ (amphoteric) > SiO₂ (acidic).

13. (c) — The ns² np⁶ shell is full, so an extra electron must go into the next shell, far from the nucleus and well screened — energy has to be supplied.

Answers and explanations — Set C
